subtype: Homesick and touch-starved in a hostel [Actor]
passage:
In my first term at the girls' hostel in Pune, what I missed most wasn't Amma's food. It was her hand. At home she'd pat my head while passing, or rest her palm on my back while I studied. Here, nobody touched me for weeks. I didn't even notice until one evening the canteen aunty brushed my arm handing me a plate, and my eyes filled up.
I felt achy all the time, like a bruise I couldn't find.
Then after our first exam, my roommate Ira threw her arms around me in the corridor. I laughed and cried at once.
After that I joined the Sunday volunteers at the animal shelter. I spend an hour brushing old dogs who lean on my legs. Ira and I link arms on the way to class. It isn't home. But I don't ache the same way anymore.

Ankita

qa.q: Where does Ankita volunteer on Sundays?
qa.a: Ankita volunteers at the animal shelter, brushing old dogs.

qa.q: What did Ankita feel when the canteen aunty brushed Ankita's arm?
qa.a: Ankita felt a sudden rush of loneliness and longing for home, strong enough to bring tears.

qa.q: Which healthy ways helped meet Ankita's need for touch?
qa.a: A friend's hug and linked arms with Ira, and brushing dogs at the shelter every Sunday.

qa.q: How might Ira have felt hugging Ankita after the exam?
qa.a: Ira was probably relieved and happy after the exam, and may have sensed that Ankita needed warmth.

grounding: It shows a young adult far from family feeling an aching loneliness for everyday touch, and finding friends and pets to meet some of that need.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Wednesday

Manoj, first-year, from Assam, has been quiet since he arrived. I often see him eating alone and on the phone with his mother late at night. Last week a senior patted his shoulder in the corridor, and Manoj jumped, then looked like he might cry. He told me later he's never been away from home and misses "just being around people who know me."
I didn't push him to talk more. I asked him to join the evening football, where the boys high-five and pile on each other after goals. I also asked him to help feed the hostel's stray dog, Kalu, who follows him everywhere now.
Today I saw him laughing on the field with his arm around a teammate. I'll keep checking on him.

Rafiq

qa.q: What is the name of the hostel's stray dog?
qa.a: The dog is called Kalu.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel when the senior patted his shoulder?
qa.a: He felt startled and suddenly emotional, almost crying, because he missed being close to people who know him.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that helped Manoj?
qa.a: Rafiq invited him into football, where friendly contact is normal, and gave him the dog to care for, instead of pushing him to talk.

qa.q: How might Manoj's mother feel if she heard he was laughing on the field?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved that he is finding friends at the hostel, even while she misses him.

grounding: It shows a young adult far from home feeling lonely and touch-starved, and how sport, a pet and friendly company meet some of that need.

passage: By October, Kiran, nineteen, had been in the Delhi hostel for two months, and the ache had settled in his chest. At home in Kochi, Amma ruffled his hair every morning. His little sister leaned on him while watching TV. Here, nobody touched him at all, except by accident in the crowded mess queue. He noticed how he lingered when the barber's hands pressed his shoulders. He felt a little ashamed of that. One evening his roommate Manoj found him staring at old family photos. 'Come play football. We need one more.' Kiran went. Someone clapped him on the back after a good pass, and he laughed out loud. The next day he started walking the hostel's stray dog, Bhoori, who leaned her whole weight against his legs. The ache didn't vanish. But it eased.

'Sudha, you've been quiet for days.'
'I'm fine, Thomas.'
'You cried at the canteen when the aunty patted your head.'
Sudha laughed shakily. 'That was embarrassing.'
'Homesick?'
'It's weird. I miss my mother's hand on my back when she walks past. My sister sleeping next to me. Here, nobody touches you for weeks.'
'That's not weird. That's human.'
She wiped her eyes.
'Would a hug help? Only if you want.'
She nodded. He hugged her briefly.
'Also, the animal shelter needs weekend volunteers. Lots of puppies who need cuddling.'
Sudha smiled properly. 'That sounds perfect.'
'And we're doing Sunday cooking in the common room. Come.'

qa.a: The aunty.

qa.a: A hug only if she wanted it, volunteering at the animal shelter, and Sunday cooking in the common room.

qa.a: He was probably concerned for his friend and wanted to help gently.

subtype: Homesick and touch-starved in a hostel [Actor]
passage: My first semester in Pune, I didn't realise how much I missed being touched until a stranger bumped my shoulder on the bus and I almost cried. At home in Nagpur, there was always someone: Ammi fixing my hair, my brothers wrestling on the floor, Nani holding my hand at the market. In the hostel, there was nothing. I felt a dull ache all the time. I'm Charu, and my friend Alka noticed first. She dragged me to a dance class where people held hands in the circle. We started cooking together on Sundays, bumping elbows in the tiny kitchen. I began hugging her goodbye after every weekend. By the end of the semester, the ache was quieter. I still missed home. But I'd found some warmth here too.

qa.q: Where did Charu study during the first semester?
qa.a: In Pune.

qa.q: What did Charu feel in the hostel?
qa.a: Charu felt a dull, lonely ache from missing the everyday touch of family.

qa.q: What helped Charu find warmth in healthy ways?
qa.a: A dance class, Sunday cooking with Alka and hugging friends goodbye.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt when Charu started hugging her goodbye?
qa.a: Alka probably felt glad and warm, seeing that Charu was less lonely.

grounding: Shows a young adult far from family feeling touch-starved and lonely, and friends, dance and shared routines meeting some of that need.

Warden's note, girls' hostel, Block C, 12 October.
Sunaina, first year, from Imphal, has been sitting alone in the common room most evenings, phone on her lap, not really watching the TV. Her roommate mentioned that Sunaina cried after a video call with her grandmother and said, "I just miss someone patting my head." Today I asked if she would like to help with the hostel's rescued cat, which needs feeding at seven. She came, and stayed half an hour with the cat curled against her. I also told her about the Tuesday badminton group that Akash from the sports office runs. She went, and came back laughing with two girls from Block A who linked arms with her on the stairs. I'll keep an eye on her through Diwali, when many go home and she won't.

qa.a: At seven.
